memory_leads.lead: The tanker sector appears to have remained burdened by severe overcapacity from the 1970s, with extensive lay-up, scrapping and depressed asset values even as oil-trade patterns kept changing.
unknowns: Exact trough years by ship size

memory_leads.lead: The Iran-Iraq War and later Tanker War made Persian Gulf shipping risk, insurance, routing, naval protection and tanker damage central market variables.
Containerization spread further across global liner trades, while carriers increasingly built hub-and-spoke networks, cellular containership fleets and dedicated terminal relationships.
unknowns: When transshipment became dominant in specific regions

memory_leads.lead: Early forms of global carrier cooperation and consortia likely expanded as lines sought scale and schedule frequency without individually owning all required vessels; conference systems still coexisted with newer competitive structures.
Dry bulk cycles remained closely tied to steelmaking raw materials, coal and grain, with fleet economics increasingly segmented among Handysize/Panamax/Capesize-type trades.
The Baltic Freight Index emerged as an important market benchmark ancestor to later Baltic dry indexes, reflecting a broader shift toward standardized freight-market price discovery.
unknowns: How quickly it became industry standard

memory_leads.lead: South Korea rose rapidly in large commercial shipbuilding, challenging Japan; European yards continued losing share in standardized tankers, bulkers and containerships while retaining niches.

Shipping finance increasingly involved specialized European and Japanese banks, tax structures and asset-backed lending, while distressed 1970s assets created opportunities for financially stronger owners.
Fuel efficiency, hull optimization and diesel propulsion became increasingly important after the oil shocks, while container ships grew gradually larger and more standardized.
Asian export growth supported expansion of container hubs such as Singapore, Hong Kong, Kaohsiung and Japanese ports, alongside growing terminal specialization and transshipment.
LNG shipping remained project-linked with long-term charters and dedicated vessels; Japanese utilities and Asian import growth were likely key demand anchors.
The Exxon Valdez spill became a major catalyst for tanker pollution regulation and public scrutiny, setting up the U.S. double-hull requirements that followed.

judgment_leads.judgment: Tanker owners likely expected any recovery to depend on scrapping/lay-up discipline because nominal fleet capacity vastly exceeded demand.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Do not use later recoveries to simplify how long the slump was expected to last.

judgment_leads.judgment: Falling oil prices may have generated mixed expectations: better oil demand and transport volumes versus persistent tanker oversupply.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Separate commodity-demand expectations from shipping-supply expectations.

judgment_leads.judgment: Container operators increasingly likely viewed network scale and terminal access as strategic advantages, but later alliance structures should not be backdated.
